changes.before: And there is one thing Laozi has that SAE lacks. Chapter 30: he who assists a ruler with the Way does not coerce the world with arms; such affairs are apt to rebound. This is a judgement about blowback, and where it appears is worth noting: it is in the judgement about going to war, not in the judgement about means. SAE's treatment of blowback is concentrated at the layer of means — §12 on how deceit suppresses one's own subjecthood, and the four mechanisms set side by side in volume three all act on means. Theorem One has no such item. It asks is it unavoidable; it does not ask how will this come back on us. The item can be taken up, and the taking has a difficulty: add will it rebound to Theorem One and Theorem One acquires a component of consequence-calculation — which is exactly what the next distinction is meant to keep it clear of. How to take it up is left open.

changes.before: This volume, like the rest of the series, keeps its correction records in the body: withdrawn propositions, narrowed claims and reductions are marked where they occurred rather than silently repaired.
